'''Michel Hénon''' ({{IPA|fr|enɔ̃|lang}}; 23 July 1931, [[Paris]] – 7 April 2013, [[Nice]]) was a French [[mathematician]] and [[astronomer]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.oca.eu/spip.php?article788 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150406013306/https://www.oca.eu/spip.php?article788 |url-status=dead |archive-date=6 April 2015 |title=[Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur&#93; Décès de Michel Hénon, Astronome à l'Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur |publisher=Oca.eu |date=18 March 2011 |accessdate=12 June 2013 }}</ref> He worked for a long time at the [[Nice Observatory]].

In astronomy, Hénon is well known for his contributions to [[stellar dynamics]]. In the late 1960s and early 1970s he made important contributions on the dynamical evolution of star clusters, in particular [[globular cluster]]s. He developed a numerical technique using [[Monte Carlo method]]s to follow the dynamical evolution of a spherical star cluster much faster than the so-called [[n-body problem|''n''-body method]]s.

In mathematics, he is well known for the [[Hénon map]], a simple discrete [[dynamical system]] that exhibits [[chaos theory|chaotic behavior]]. He published a two-volume work on the [[restricted three-body problem]].

In 1978 he was awarded the ''[[Prix Jean Ricard]]''.

The [[European Space Agency]]'s ''[[HENON]]'' spacecraft is named after him and will use a type of orbit he developed.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ESA’s first stand-alone deep-space CubeSat Henon takes shape |url=https://www.esa.int/Enabling_Support/Space_Engineering_Technology/ESA_s_first_stand-alone_deep-space_CubeSat_Henon_takes_shape |access-date=2025-11-07 |website=www.esa.int |language=en}}</ref>
